Thirteen English- and Korean-language databases were searched through May 2026 for RCTs of community-dwelling older adults with a study-sample mean or median age ≥65 years. Interventions were classified using a theoretically informed operational framework. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2. Pairwise and Bayesian network meta-analyses estimated standardized mean differences (SMDs); certainty was assessed using GRADE, with SUCRA rankings considered secondary. Seventy-one RCTs (12,159 participants) were included. The overall pairwise effect favored activity-based interventions (SMD=0.59, 95% CI 0.45-0.73), but heterogeneity was substantial and the prediction interval crossed the null; certainty was very low. Category-specific pairwise estimates were 0.68 (0.27-1.08) for self-directed, 0.61 (0.43-0.78) for physical, and 0.46 (0.21-0.72) for social activities, all with very-low-certainty evidence. In the network meta-analysis, low-certainty evidence suggested that all three categories may improve QoL versus no treatment: self-directed SMD=0.78 (95% CrI 0.25-1.32; SUCRA 82.5%), physical 0.73 (0.46-1.00; 79.6%), and social 0.40 (0.11-0.69; 37.6%). Excluding high-risk studies yielded an overall pairwise estimate of 0.53 (0.37-0.69); the estimate for physical activities remained 0.61, whereas the estimates for social and self-directed activities were 0.43 and 0.45. Evidence does not establish superiority of one activity category. Findings remain limited by heterogeneity, risk of bias, potential publication bias, and sparse direct active comparisons. VAT and WC were primary outcomes; SAT, body fat percentage, BMI, body weight, fat mass, and VO₂max were secondary outcomes. Hedges' g was synthesized using three-level random-effects models to accommodate dependent effect sizes within studies. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool. Twenty-one trials involving 1,754 participants were included. Exercise interventions were associated with lower VAT (g = -0.725, 95% CI [-1.120, -0.330], p < 0.001) and WC (g = -0.692, 95% CI [-0.984, -0.400], p < 0.001). HIIT showed the largest VAT point estimate (g = -1.332, 95% CI [-1.874, -0.789]), but between-modality differences were not significant for VAT ( p = 0.116) or WC ( p = 0.184). Prediction intervals for both primary outcomes crossed the null, indicating uncertainty across study settings. Secondary outcomes generally favored exercise. Exercise-based interventions were associated with reductions in VAT and WC, but current evidence does not establish the superiority of any single modality. Although HIIT showed the largest VAT point estimate, non-significant between-modality tests and prediction intervals crossing the null preclude firm conclusions about an optimal exercise modality.
